bigPicture: Investors kept selling AI-linked shares a day before Nvidia's results: the Nasdaq was down about 2% in New York trading, while Europe slipped only slightly and Warsaw's WIG20 ended flat. Expectations of more interest-rate rises spread from the US to the UK and euro area, pushing gold to a one-year low and UK two-year borrowing costs above 5%. Washington issued a rule to stop Chinese firms renting US AI chips through foreign data centres as President Trump left for Asia, where he is due to meet Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin on 19 November. In the Middle East another tanker was hit near Hormuz and Yemen's Houthis edged closer to Aden, but oil fell on expectations of a supply surplus.

glossary.def: The overall mood of investors, from optimism to fear, which affects how much they are willing to pay for assets.
glossary.example: Fear about AI spending hit chip shares before Nvidia's results.

glossary.def: The percentage fall of an asset or index from its previous peak to a later low.
glossary.example: Gold's drawdown from its January record reached 31.5% on 16 November.

glossary.def: Price divided by the average of the last ten years of inflation-adjusted earnings; a measure of how expensive a stock market is.
glossary.example: ChartRow estimated the S&P 500's CAPE at 38.6 on 13 November 2026, against a long-run median of 16.6.

glossary.def: An index of the S&P 500's expected volatility over the next 30 days, derived from option prices and nicknamed the 'fear gauge'.
glossary.example: The VIX closed at 19.30 on 13 November.

glossary.def: A period when an asset's price rises far above what expected future income can justify, usually ending in a sharp fall.
glossary.example: The Nasdaq lost about 78% after the dot-com bubble burst in 2000–02.

glossary.def: A demand from a broker for more cash when falling prices shrink the investor's own money in a position bought with borrowed funds.
glossary.example: Margin calls can force sales that deepen a crash.

glossary.def: A US regulation that takes effect before the public comment process is finished.
glossary.example: Commerce issued its AI-chip remote-access rule as an interim final rule.

glossary.def: Government rules that require licences, or ban sales, for sending certain goods or technology abroad.
glossary.example: The US limits exports of advanced AI chips to China.

glossary.def: The absence of continuous transmission of a disease in a country for at least 12 months; imported cases can still occur.
glossary.example: The US lost its measles-elimination status after transmission continued for a year.

glossary.def: Hostile actions below open war, such as sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation or using migrants to put pressure on a border.
glossary.example: Estonia linked an arson attempt on a drone maker to Russian military intelligence.

glossary.def: Inflation excluding the most volatile prices, usually food and energy, used to judge underlying price pressure.
glossary.example: Poland's core inflation fell to 2.9% in October 2026.

glossary.def: A change in a year-on-year rate caused by an unusual price movement 12 months earlier rather than by current prices.
glossary.example: Canada's 30.9% annual petrol inflation partly reflects a sharp fall in October 2025.

glossary.def: The risks and costs that stop investors from correcting mispriced assets, for example because a bubble can keep growing longer than a bettor can wait.
glossary.example: Short-sellers betting against internet shares in 1999 often lost money before the crash.

In Europe Siemens, Infineon and ASML fell, miners such as Anglo American dropped on weaker metal prices, and Stellantis hit a 52-week low, while Novo Nordisk rose on new obesity-drug data. In Warsaw KGHM fell 3.3% with copper and silver, but GPW jumped 5.5% after beating profit forecasts and the WIG20 was flat.

stories.everyday: Many Polish pension (PPK/IKE) and ETF savers own US tech shares through global index funds, so the value of those savings drops on days like this. Polish shares were barely touched: the WIG20 ended flat.
stories.rankWhy: The AI share sell-off hits the world's largest stock market and the savings and pension funds of hundreds of millions of people, a day before Nvidia's results.
stories.title: Wall Street slides as the AI sell-off deepens: Nasdaq down about 2% before Nvidia's results and Anthropic's market debut
stories.what: US shares fell for another day on Monday. At 1:13 p.m. New York time (19:13 Warsaw) the S&P 500 was down 1.59% at 7,441.56, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite down 2.19% at 24,586.82 and the Dow Jones down 1.00% at 51,822.84 (Reuters data via MarketScreener). Nine of the S&P 500's 11 sectors fell, led by technology (about −2%); the Philadelphia semiconductor index lost 3.7%, Intel 6.4% and Micron 5.8%, while Nvidia fell between about 2% and 4.5% during the day (Reuters; Yahoo Finance). Nvidia reports quarterly results on Tuesday after the US close, its first since co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive last week, and Anthropic's shares are expected to start trading on Thursday. These are intraday figures; the US close comes at 22:00 Warsaw time, after this edition.
stories.why: Reuters, quoted by MarketScreener, linked the fall to investors cutting exposure to AI-linked shares before two events that will test confidence in AI spending, plus high borrowing costs and last week's hotter-than-expected US inflation data. Futures markets now fully price a Federal Reserve rate rise in December (CME FedWatch); higher rates make far-off future profits, which drive tech valuations, worth less today. The Financial Times reported that Huang is in talks with allies about a possible return, and President Trump said he would not oppose it (Reuters via MarketScreener).

stories.everyday: Higher interest rates abroad tend to strengthen the dollar: USD/PLN was back at about 4.00 on Monday morning, which makes dollar-priced goods such as fuel and electronics a little dearer in Poland. Gold-coin buyers have seen prices fall by almost a third since January.
stories.rankWhy: Expectations of more interest-rate rises in the US, UK and euro area raise borrowing costs for governments, firms and households across many countries and are pushing gold to a one-year low.
stories.title: Rate-rise bets spread: gold hits a one-year low, UK two-year borrowing costs top 5% and ECB officials eye a December hike
stories.what: Gold fell to $3,830.74 an ounce on Monday, its lowest since 2 October 2025 and 31.5% below its January record of $5,594.82, putting it on course for its worst year since 2015 (Reuters via MarketScreener). Markets fully price a 0.25-point Federal Reserve rise in December, with a small chance of 0.5 points (CME FedWatch, cited by Reuters). In Britain the two-year government bond (gilt) yield rose above 5% for the first time since 2023 after Bank of England chief economist Huw Pill told the Financial Times 'we have further to go' (City AM). In the euro area, ECB policymaker Gediminas Šimkus said a December rate rise is his central scenario (Newsquawk). Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, speaking in San Francisco, focused on AI's possible effects on growth and jobs and did not comment on interest rates (AP via CP24).
stories.why: Inflation pushed up by the Iran war's oil shock and, according to several Fed officials, by AI-related demand for chips, power and copper is leading central banks to signal more rises (AP; Reuters). Gold pays no interest, so when interest rates and the dollar rise, holding it becomes less attractive; Reuters also cited weaker coin and bar demand and that Poland's central bank, the most active official buyer, likely stopped buying after reaching its 700-tonne target.

stories.everyday: Few households notice directly, but such rules shape where AI data centres are built and how expensive AI services become. Poland's own plans for AI 'gigafactories' depend on access to US chips.
stories.rankWhy: A new US export rule affects every data-centre operator worldwide that rents advanced AI computing power, and directly touches Nvidia, China's AI firms and five emerging economies.
stories.title: US moves to stop China renting American AI chips through foreign data centres
stories.what: On Monday the US Commerce Department issued an interim final rule (a rule that takes effect before public comments are finished) requiring a licence to export advanced AI chips and servers to any data centre in the world that may sell computing power to companies from China or other restricted countries (TechCrunch). It applies to data centres above a set size, roughly equal to 750 Nvidia H100 or H200 chips, and existing operators must obtain licences within 90 days of it taking effect (TechCrunch). Exports of advanced chips to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand now need a licence (CBS News). Commerce said the rule ensures existing restrictions 'cannot be circumvented through remote computing' (CBS News); it also rescinds the Biden-era January 2025 'AI Diffusion Rule' (TechCrunch).
stories.why: Until now, Chinese firms barred from buying top chips could rent their power from data centres abroad. The rule came days after Nvidia's Jensen Huang resigned amid reports of a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, which raised concern about chips reaching China via third countries (CBS News; TechCrunch). It was issued as President Trump left for Asia, where he is due to meet Xi Jinping; Trump said on Monday that 'selling the other chips is a good thing' (CBS News).

stories.everyday: Lower crude prices feed through to Polish petrol and diesel prices with a delay of days to weeks, though a stronger dollar partly offsets this because oil is priced in dollars.
stories.rankWhy: Attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz threaten one of the world's key oil routes, but this time oil prices fell because the market now expects a supply surplus.
stories.title: Tanker hit by a projectile leaving the Strait of Hormuz, yet oil falls as the IEA expects a surplus
stories.what: The UK's maritime security agency UKMTO said a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile while leaving the Strait of Hormuz at 05:58 GMT (06:58 Warsaw) on Monday, causing an engine-room fire; no one was hurt and all crew were accounted for (ABC News; Newsquawk). Iran's Revolutionary Guards had claimed several tankers hit mines in the strait since Sunday; those claims have not been independently confirmed. The US says more than 20 navy ships are enforcing its blockade of Iran's ports (ABC News), but reports on Monday said Washington was not considering imminent strikes on Iran (Newsquawk). Brent crude nevertheless fell about 1–2% to roughly $94–95 a barrel (HDFC Sky; Newsquawk).
stories.why: Oil traders are weighing the attacks against the International Energy Agency's forecast that the market returns to a surplus in the fourth quarter, with supply about 1.7 million barrels a day above demand, and its finding that shipments through Hormuz have nearly returned to pre-war levels (HDFC Sky, citing the IEA). When expected supply exceeds demand, prices tend to fall even if risks remain.

stories.everyday: Much of Europe's trade with Asia passes through Bab al-Mandeb and the Suez Canal; renewed risk there can raise shipping and insurance costs, and with them some import prices in Poland.
stories.rankWhy: A Houthi advance towards Aden and the Bab al-Mandeb strait threatens Yemen's government and a sea route that has become more important while Hormuz is disrupted.
stories.title: Yemen: government forces pull back from near Bab al-Mandeb as the Houthis edge closer to Aden
stories.what: Yemeni government forces withdrew from Dhubab airport and nearby territory close to the Bab al-Mandeb strait on Sunday to help defend Aden, the government's temporary seat, Al Jazeera reported. The Houthis have reached Tor al-Baha, about 80 km from Aden (Al Jazeera); a government military source cited in this morning's edition put them about 70 km away, so sources differ. A government military spokesman called the move a tactical redeployment. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted Houthi drones over Mecca and Medina and missiles aimed at Riyadh, which the Houthis called a fabrication (Anadolu). Yemen's parliament approved a bill designating the Houthis a terrorist organisation (Anadolu).
stories.why: Bab al-Mandeb links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and has become more important for world trade since the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed during the US-Israel war with Iran, Al Jazeera noted. Analysts quoted by Al Jazeera said Houthi gains threaten to cut the government's coastal supply routes, giving the group more leverage over shipping.

stories.everyday: Arms-control talks and US–China trade relations affect the security climate in Europe and the prices of electronics and other imports from Asia.
stories.rankWhy: A trip ending in the first-ever US–China–Russia leaders' talks on nuclear weapons could shape security and trade for much of the world.
stories.title: Trump leaves for Asia ahead of the first three-way summit with Xi and Putin, on nuclear weapons
stories.what: President Donald Trump left on Monday for Asia, starting in Manila, where the White House says he will sign a trade deal with Thailand, then going to Shenzhen in China for the APEC summit (AP via PBS). The Kremlin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin, Xi and Trump will meet in Shenzhen on 19 November, on the sidelines of APEC (Anadolu). US officials say the three-way talks will cover nuclear weapons and not Russia's war in Ukraine; China's foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning called them of 'groundbreaking significance' (AP via PBS). Elon Musk is travelling with the president (AP).
stories.why: The US, Russia and China hold most of the world's nuclear weapons, and there has been no three-way framework to limit them. The trip comes as Trump's party lost both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections and as the US tightens chip rules, so any trade or technology deal with Xi would be watched closely by markets (AP via PBS).

stories.everyday: Sanctions on Russian energy have helped keep fuel prices higher across Europe since 2022, but they also reduce the risk of Poland depending on Russian supplies.
stories.rankWhy: New EU listings tighten pressure on Russia's oil exports and hybrid operations and set up a 22nd sanctions package before Christmas.
stories.title: EU foreign ministers approve about 140 new Russia sanctions listings and prepare a 22nd package
stories.what: EU foreign ministers meeting in Brussels on Monday approved new sanctions against Russia: France's foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot spoke of 145 provisions, while TASS, citing a source, put the number at about 140 people and entities across three lists, so counts differ slightly (UNN; TASS). Targets include Wildberries chief executive Tatyana Kim and an oil terminal in St Petersburg (Barrot via UNN); the lists cover cyber and hybrid attacks and foreign-owned tankers, with travel bans and asset freezes (TASS). Ireland's foreign minister Helen McEntee, whose country holds the EU presidency, said a 22nd package is being finalised for discussion later this week; RFE/RL's Rikard Jozwiak reported the aim is approval by Christmas (UNN).
stories.why: Sanctions aim to cut the money Russia earns to fund its war, especially from oil shipped by the so-called shadow fleet of old tankers with unclear ownership. Barrot said France and the UK will hold a conference on the shadow fleet on 4 December (UNN).

stories.everyday: Poland, like other EU countries, funds humanitarian aid for Gaza through the EU budget; the story also shapes EU–Israel relations.
stories.rankWhy: Hundreds of thousands of displaced people in Gaza face the first winter storms in flooded tents while aid supplies wait at the border.
stories.title: EU commissioner says children are dying of hypothermia in Gaza as ministers press Israel to let tents in
stories.what: EU crisis-management commissioner Hadja Lahbib said on Monday that families in Gaza are exposed to freezing rain and children are dying from hypothermia, and criticised Israel for allowing 'dual-use' supplies such as generators and tent poles in only once a week (Irish Times). Ireland's foreign minister Helen McEntee called it unacceptable that food and equipment are waiting at the border (Irish Times). The foreign ministers of Australia, Canada, Italy and the UK jointly urged Israel to admit 150,000 tents and other supplies before winter, after the first storm flooded tens of thousands of shelters (Anadolu; Irish Times). The reports give no exact death toll.
stories.why: Israel says dual-use items, goods with both civilian and military uses, could be used by Hamas fighters, so it restricts them (Irish Times). Aid agencies say the restrictions leave people who lost their homes in the two-year war without adequate shelter as temperatures fall.

stories.everyday: Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known. Poland also has pockets of low vaccination, and travellers can carry it across borders, so two doses of the MMR vaccine (about 97% effective) matter here too.
stories.rankWhy: Losing measles-elimination status shows a highly contagious disease is spreading continuously again in a country of 340 million people.
stories.title: The US loses its measles-elimination status after 26 years, health experts say
stories.what: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the WHO's regional office for the Americas, has concluded that measles has re-established sustained transmission in the United States, which had been declared measles-free in 2000 (WBUR; Salt Lake Tribune via KFF Health News). Researchers told KFF Health News a public announcement was planned for Tuesday. Over the past two years more than 8,000 people fell ill in US outbreaks and more than 830 were hospitalised; states have reported 13 measles-associated deaths (Salt Lake Tribune). A West Texas outbreak that began in 2025 spread to Mexico and sickened more than 4,500 people in the two countries, killing at least 16.
stories.why: A country loses elimination status when one chain of measles transmission continues for 12 months or more; a Utah outbreak passed the one-year mark in June (Salt Lake Tribune). Outbreaks usually fade when at least 95% of a community is immunised; the health department blamed vaccination gaps that predate the current administration, while critics point to cuts in immunisation programmes (Salt Lake Tribune).

stories.everyday: Poland faces similar hybrid threats; this morning's edition reported Polish rail investigators linking incidents on the Warsaw–Dorohusk line to terrorism. Border closures can also affect regional trade and travel.
stories.rankWhy: A NATO member on Poland's side of the EU's eastern border plans to shut all crossings with Russia, a sign of rising hybrid threats in the Baltic region.
stories.title: Estonia plans to close all border crossings with Russia from 1 December after a sabotage attempt
stories.what: Estonia's foreign ministry announced plans to close all three operating crossings with Russia, at Narva, Koidula and Luhamaa, from 1 December; the cabinet is expected to decide this week and to settle whether the closure is temporary or indefinite (Meduza). The move follows an attempted arson attack overnight on 14 November on Threod Systems, an Estonian drone maker; eight Latvian residents were detained and five arrested, and Estonian security services said Russian military intelligence organised it (Meduza). The Kremlin called the accusations baseless. Foreign minister Margus Tsahkna said Russia's hostile actions have a price.
stories.why: Baltic and Nordic states say Russia uses sabotage, arson and migration pressure as 'hybrid' tactics below the level of open war. Prime Minister Kristen Michal said border guards are prepared for a possible 'migration attack' in response (Meduza). Lithuania's president backed the decision and did not rule out similar steps.

stories.everyday: Slower core price growth means services and everyday non-food goods are getting dearer less quickly; it also supports the outlook for stable instalments on mortgages linked to Polish reference rates.
stories.rankWhy: Falling core inflation in Poland shapes the central bank's rate decisions, which set the cost of most Polish mortgages and loans.
stories.title: Poland's core inflation falls to 2.9% in October, the lowest since February
stories.what: Core inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, fell to 2.9% year on year in October from 3.1% in September, the National Bank of Poland (NBP) reported on Monday (finwire; managerplus). Two other NBP core measures also fell: excluding administered prices to 3.5% from 4.1%, and excluding the most volatile prices to 3.3% from 4.0%, while the trimmed mean stayed at 2.8% (finwire). Headline consumer price inflation was 3.5% in October; the NBP reference rate is 3.75% (finwire).
stories.why: Central banks watch core inflation because food and energy prices swing with weather and world markets that monetary policy cannot control; core shows the more persistent trend. A falling core rate eases pressure on the NBP's Monetary Policy Council to raise rates at a time when the Fed, Bank of England and some ECB officials are talking about rises.

stories.everyday: COP outcomes guide EU climate rules such as carbon pricing, which affect heating and electricity bills in Poland.
stories.rankWhy: Climate talks among nearly 200 countries are entering their final week, with finance and fossil fuels unresolved.
stories.title: COP31 climate talks enter their final week as Australia circulates a first draft deal
stories.what: The UN climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, which runs 9–20 November, entered its final week with ministers arriving for Tuesday's high-level segment (UN News). Australia, the co-host and lead negotiator, circulated a first draft of an overarching 'cover' decision late on Monday, but countries disagree over its contents and even whether it should exist (UN News). The main disputes are who pays for climate action and adaptation, wording on moving away from fossil fuels, protections for workers in the energy transition and the timetable of the next IPCC science report (UN News). A UN University expert said the first week was slow and he expects the talks to run over time. Climate Home News reported that Saudi Arabia opposes referring to Brazil's roadmap for moving away from fossil fuels, and that many developing countries want adaptation finance tripled to at least $120 billion a year by 2035.
stories.why: COP decisions need consensus among almost 200 countries, so oil producers, rich countries and vulnerable nations can each block wording. Rich countries' budgets are under strain from defence and energy costs, making finance pledges harder.

stories.everyday: ECB decisions move the euro and European interest rates, which influence the złoty and the cost of euro loans for Polish firms.
stories.rankWhy: The next ECB president will set monetary policy for the 21 euro-area countries and influence rates across Europe, including Poland.
stories.title: Spain's Hernández de Cos emerges as favourite to succeed Lagarde at the ECB
stories.what: Former Dutch central bank chief Klaas Knot is expected to withdraw from the race to become European Central Bank president, the Dutch newspaper de Volkskrant reported, citing diplomats; his spokesperson declined to comment (LaPresse; Newsquawk). Germany and France have reportedly agreed in principle that Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos, a former governor of the Bank of Spain, should get the job (LaPresse). Christine Lagarde is due to step down in February 2027. Separately, euro-area industrial production fell 1.5% year on year, more than the 0.2% drop expected (Newsquawk).
stories.why: ECB presidents are chosen by EU governments, so the post is part of wider bargaining over top EU jobs; the chief economist and markets-supervision posts on the ECB board also fall vacant soon (LaPresse). The choice matters because the ECB is weighing a December rate rise despite weak industry.

stories.everyday: Poland supplies electricity and equipment to Ukraine and hosts many Ukrainian refugees; heavier attacks in winter can increase both needs.
stories.rankWhy: Russian attacks on Ukraine's power grid leave hundreds of thousands without electricity as winter begins, while Ukraine's drone war hits Russia.
stories.title: Ukraine warns of a new Russian missile strike as attacks cut power to hundreds of thousands
stories.what: President Volodymyr Zelensky urged Ukrainians on Monday evening to take air-raid alerts seriously overnight and on Tuesday, saying intelligence showed Russia had prepared a new strike (UNN). A Russian attack on power lines and substations in the Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions left hundreds of thousands of people without electricity (Il Sole 24 Ore). Russia's Moscow-installed head of Crimea said the Crimean Bridge was struck and traffic restricted, and Russia's defence ministry said it shot down 1,336 Ukrainian drones overnight, one of the largest attacks of the year (Il Sole 24 Ore). Ukraine and the EU are finalising an emergency winter aid package with generators and buses (Il Sole 24 Ore).
stories.why: Both sides target energy: Russia aims at Ukraine's grid to weaken civilian morale and industry in winter, while Ukraine strikes Russian refineries and logistics to reduce fuel output and export income. Zelensky said Russia receives dozens of ballistic missiles a month from North Korea (UNN).

stories.everyday: A working constitutional court matters to citizens because it decides whether laws, from taxes to rights, comply with the constitution.
stories.rankWhy: The dispute over Poland's Constitutional Tribunal affects the rule of law and the validity of court rulings for 38 million people.
stories.title: Presidential talks on the Constitutional Tribunal agree to draft constitutional changes, without KO and the Left
stories.what: Talks on the Constitutional Tribunal at the Belweder palace on Monday were chaired by Zbigniew Bogucki, head of the President's Chancellery; President Karol Nawrocki did not attend (Rzeczpospolita). Right-wing and conservative groups took part along with two governing-coalition parties, PSL and Polska 2050, while Civic Coalition (KO) and the Left stayed away (Rzeczpospolita). Participants agreed to start work now on a joint draft amending the constitution's provisions on the Tribunal, and a follow-up meeting is set for Wednesday at 17:00 (Rzeczpospolita). Bogucki noted that the groups whose votes are needed to change the constitution were absent.
stories.why: The Tribunal has been at the centre of a long political dispute over how its judges were appointed, and the main parties disagree on how to resolve it. Changing the Polish constitution needs a two-thirds majority in the Sejm, which is impossible without KO, so the talks' outcome is uncertain (Bogucki himself noted the missing votes).

stories.everyday: The same oil-price shock is lifting fuel costs in Poland; comparing 'headline' and 'excluding energy' figures helps show whether price rises are spreading beyond fuel.
stories.rankWhy: Steady Canadian inflation matters mainly for Canada's 41 million people and its central bank.
stories.title: Canada's inflation holds at 3.1% in October as petrol prices jump 30.9% from a year ago
stories.what: Statistics Canada said consumer prices rose 3.1% year on year in October, the same as in September and slightly below the 3.2% economists expected (Statistics Canada; Newsquawk). Petrol prices were 30.9% higher than a year earlier, which the agency attributed mainly to a base-year effect, while prices excluding energy rose 2.0%.
stories.why: A base-year effect means a yearly rate changes because of what happened 12 months earlier: petrol fell sharply in October 2025, so that fall no longer pulls this year's comparison down. The gap between 3.1% overall and 2.0% excluding energy shows how much of Canada's inflation comes from oil prices.

stories.everyday: For Polish readers, it is similar to how the Warsaw exchange has sought regional links in Central and Eastern Europe.
stories.rankWhy: A cross-border stake links two of Africa's main stock exchanges, with modest immediate effect.
stories.title: Nigeria's stock exchange group buys 10% of the Nairobi Securities Exchange
stories.what: Nigerian Exchange Group (NGX Group), owner of the Lagos stock exchange, announced on Monday that it has bought a 10% stake in the Nairobi Securities Exchange; the price and seller were not disclosed (Rio Times). Chairman Umaru Kwairanga called it a long-term step towards closer financial ties between West and East Africa. NGX Group has previously invested in the Ethiopian Securities Exchange.
stories.why: Africa's stock markets are small and fragmented; owning stakes in each other can make it easier to share trading technology and, eventually, to list or trade shares across borders.

stories.everyday: Strong trading volumes mean more Poles are investing in shares directly or through funds.
stories.rankWhy: Better-than-expected profits at Warsaw's stock exchange reflect high trading activity on the Polish market.
stories.title: Warsaw Stock Exchange shares jump after third-quarter profit beats forecasts
stories.what: Shares of GPW, the company that runs the Warsaw Stock Exchange, rose about 4–6% on Monday after it reported third-quarter net profit of 70.3 million zł, above a consensus of about 63 million, with revenue up 17% to 158.5 million zł (FXMAG). FXMAG linked the result to high trading volumes. The WIG20 index ended flat at 4,302.04 points, just above Friday's record close (ISBnews via Investing.com).
stories.why: An exchange earns fees on every trade, so record trading volumes in Warsaw this year translate into higher revenue.

stories.everyday: Instability in South Sudan adds to refugee flows in East Africa, which the EU helps fund.
stories.rankWhy: A further delay to South Sudan's first election since independence affects about 11 million people and fragile peace.
stories.title: South Sudan delays its first-ever national election again, to 11 February 2027
stories.what: South Sudan's National Elections Commission set 11 February 2027 for the vote, which had been scheduled for 22 December 2026; spokesperson Josephine Achiro Fortelo told Reuters the timetable followed consultations (TimesLive/Reuters). AllAfrica reported results are expected on 15 February. In September the UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan said conditions for a peaceful, credible election were lacking.
stories.why: The commission said more time is needed for voter registration and logistics. The country, independent since 2011, has repeatedly postponed elections amid violence between forces loyal to President Salva Kiir and supporters of detained former vice-president Riek Machar (AllAfrica).

stories.everyday: Indonesia is a major supplier of nickel, palm oil and coal, so political stability there matters for world commodity markets.
stories.rankWhy: The choice of a new vice-president matters for the politics of Indonesia, a country of about 280 million people.
stories.title: Indonesia delays the vote on a new vice-president to 9 December after Gibran's resignation
stories.what: Indonesia's parliament moved the vote to choose a successor to Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the eldest son of former president Joko Widodo, from 2 December to 9 December because President Prabowo Subianto wants more time to consult his coalition (Rio Times). Gibran resigned last week without giving a reason, after two court rulings on his education papers; Prabowo must name two candidates by 25 November.
stories.why: Under Indonesia's constitution, when the vice-presidency falls vacant the president proposes two candidates and the People's Consultative Assembly (MPR) elects one.

stories.everyday: The war has displaced millions; the EU, including Poland, funds humanitarian aid in Sudan and neighbouring countries.
stories.rankWhy: Fighting in Sudan's Kordofan region continues a war that has created one of the world's largest displacement crises.
stories.title: Sudan's army says it has taken five areas from the RSF in West Kordofan
stories.what: The Sudanese army said it seized five areas from the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in West Kordofan (Anadolu); the claim could not be independently verified. Al Jazeera reported on 14 November that the army had taken several strategic villages, including the West Kordofan town of al-Khuwai, and broken the RSF siege of al-Obeid, and that some groups have defected from the RSF.
stories.why: Kordofan links Darfur, held largely by the RSF, with the army-held east of the country, so control of its roads and towns shapes supply lines for both sides.

stories.everyday: Youth unemployment and housing costs are concerns for young people in Poland too.
stories.rankWhy: A youth protest movement in Germany's capital shows social tensions but had limited wider effect.
stories.title: At least 20 arrested at a 'Gen Z' protest march in Berlin
stories.what: Police in Berlin said at least 20 people were arrested during a 'Gen Z' protest march over the weekend (Anadolu; Tribune Online).
stories.why: Youth-led 'Gen Z' protests, often organised on social media, have spread across several countries in the past two years, typically over the cost of living, jobs and trust in politics.

stories.everyday: Travellers flying to or via the US from Poland faced knock-on delays and cancellations.
stories.rankWhy: A nationwide US air-traffic outage disrupted travel for millions over the weekend, with effects fading by Monday.
stories.title: US flights recover after Friday's nationwide ground stop, blamed on faulty air-traffic equipment
stories.what: US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said he expected air traffic to return to normal on Monday after a communications outage forced a nationwide ground stop on Friday (Anadolu). More than 14,000 flights were cancelled on Friday and Saturday and nearly 2,300 on Sunday, and some cancellations continued into Monday (ABC7). FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford blamed faulty equipment; Duffy said the ability of air-traffic-control routers to broadcast data had been turned off and is under investigation (ABC7).
stories.why: US air-traffic control depends on networks that, when a key system fails, force controllers to halt departures to keep aircraft safely separated, and the backlog takes days to clear. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on Friday there was no indication of an attack, though a cyberattack had not been ruled out at that point (ABC7).

stories.everyday: US factory demand matters for European suppliers, including German industry, which buys many Polish components.
stories.rankWhy: A regional US factory survey gives an early, limited signal about American manufacturing.
stories.title: New York factory activity index slows far more than expected
stories.what: The New York Fed's Empire State manufacturing index fell to 7.8 in November, well below the 18.0 economists expected (Newsquawk). A reading above zero still means more firms in the region reported improving than worsening conditions.
stories.why: Surveys like this are among the first data each month, so markets use them as an early hint of how US industry is coping with high interest rates and costs; a single regional survey is volatile and can be revised by later data.

stories.everyday: Thailand is a supplier of electronics, car parts and food; slower Asian growth tends to lower demand for commodities and can ease some import prices in Europe.
stories.rankWhy: Slower growth in Thailand, a major Southeast Asian economy and manufacturing hub, has mostly regional effects.
stories.title: Thailand's economy grows just 0.3% in the third quarter, below forecasts
stories.what: Thailand's economy grew 0.3% from the previous quarter in July–September, below the 0.7% forecast, according to the Rio Times Asia brief. Japan's economy shrank 0.1% at an annualised rate in the same quarter, and China's October retail sales rose only 0.4% (Rio Times).
stories.why: Weak demand from China and higher energy costs since the Iran war weigh on Asia's export-led economies. Trump is due to sign a trade deal with Thailand in Manila this week (AP via PBS).

stories.everyday: Trust in health institutions affects vaccination rates in every country, including Poland.
stories.rankWhy: A study on threats against public-health leaders highlights a trend with limited immediate measurable effect.
stories.title: Study: most US public-health leaders faced harassment or threats after COVID-19
stories.what: A study reported by WOSU found that harassment of public-health officials has been widespread since the COVID-19 pandemic; WOWO reported that 76% of public-health leaders surveyed had faced harassment or threats.
stories.why: Researchers warn that threats push experienced officials to quit, which can weaken responses to outbreaks such as the measles spread reported in this edition.

stories.everyday: Shows how big scientific instruments often produce discoveries beyond their original purpose.
stories.rankWhy: An unexpected scientific find with no direct effect on daily life.
stories.title: Europe's Euclid space telescope discovers its first comet
stories.what: The European Space Agency said its Euclid telescope found a previously unknown comet, C/2026 S1, moving between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn about 1.3 billion km away (Space.com). University of Helsinki scientist Mikko Pöntinen spotted it in images taken on 16–24 September. Euclid was built to study dark energy and dark matter, not comets.
stories.why: Large sky surveys capture huge numbers of images, and moving objects such as comets show up as streaks that software and scientists can pick out.

stories.everyday: AI tools for science could, over time, shorten the development of new medicines and materials.
stories.rankWhy: A new AI tool for scientists with limited immediate effect beyond research labs.
stories.title: Nvidia releases open AI models and data to help build 'science agents'
stories.what: Nvidia launched 'Nemotron for Science' on Monday, a package of an AI model, a chemistry dataset of nearly 50,000 questions and training recipes for building AI agents for scientific research (company release via GlobeNewswire). Partners including Argonne National Laboratory and Japan's RIKEN said they are using the tools.
stories.why: AI companies are competing to show that their models can speed up research in chemistry and biology, which could justify their large spending on computing.

stories.everyday: Poland is one of Europe's most Catholic countries, so papal visits and messages are widely followed here.
stories.rankWhy: A papal visit draws crowds and attention in Peru with little wider measurable effect.
stories.title: Pope Leo XIV continues his visit to Peru, where he once served as a missionary
stories.what: Pope Leo XIV, on a visit to Peru running from 11 to 17 November (Andina), flew from Chiclayo to Cusco, celebrated Mass in Pucallpa and returned to Lima on Sunday; hundreds of people queued overnight for his next Mass (Rio Times).
stories.why: Before becoming pope, Leo XIV worked in Peru and served in the diocese of Chiclayo, which he is revisiting, so the trip carries personal as well as religious significance (MercoPress; UCA News).

stories.everyday: A light story for football fans.
stories.rankWhy: A sporting curiosity with no wider effect.
stories.title: Ronaldinho, 46, returns to competitive football with Italian third-tier club Ravenna
stories.what: Brazilian former world player of the year Ronaldinho started for Serie C club Ravenna in a 2-0 derby win over Forlì, playing the first half, his first official match since September 2015 (Anadolu).
stories.why: Lower-league clubs sometimes sign famous veterans to attract crowds and sponsors.
